summary: Module 6 VERIFY answers. Bug #10 causal chain (initial job failure -> API down): (1) record_click job fails when insert_click hits the DB (e.g., table lock, connection error) -- the first failure is ordinary; (2) autoretry_for=(Exception,) with retry_backoff=True and max_retries=3 makes Celery re-raise and redeliver the job; (3) each retry runs insert_click again, which opens a NEW SessionLocal() -- a fresh check-out from the shared pool; (4) if the failure condition persists, every retry cycle keeps requesting connections while earlier ones are held; (5) the worker and the API share the SAME engine/SessionLocal pool (database.py creates one engine, no pool isolation between processes); (6) pool exhaustion: all checked-out slots are now held by worker retries, new check-outs (including the API's get_db()) block waiting; (7) every API request that needs the DB parks on the pool -> the API stops responding -> 'API down'. Longest cause-to-symptom gap: the worker's DB insert failure to the API edge, crossing ~4 layers (DB -> worker process -> shared pool -> API process) -- a classic cascading failure. Bug #9 invisibility in dev: developers create and read links constantly but rarely 'delete then access within the TTL window'; the stale entry self-heals after settings.redirect_cache_ttl_seconds (5 min) expires, so manual QA sessions -- which are short and rarely revisit a just-deleted link -- never observe the 5-minute window of stale redirects; the bug 'fixes itself after 5 minutes', which is exactly why it never got noticed and why lowering the TTL is the wrong fix (it shrinks the window, it does not close it). Correct fix = explicit invalidation on delete/update: the fork's cache.py invalidate_redirect_target INCRs the redirect:ver: token AND deletes the key, and get_redirect_target rejects any payload whose version does not match the current token -- the fix I built in M3. One monitoring alert for Bug #10: DB connection pool utilization (checked-out / pool max) crossing a sustained high-water mark (e.g., >80% for 30s). Reasoning: it is the earliest signal in the chain that directly predicts API unavailability -- retry rate spikes first, but pool saturation is the step immediately before the API parks on get_db(), so it is the metric that wakes you with time to act; a bigger pool is the symptom fix (buys seconds, storm still wins), the real remedy is bounded retries with backoff plus pool isolation between worker and API so a failing job cannot starve user traffic.
evidence: Bug #10 chain traced from job failure to API down across 4 layers
Bug #9 root cause: TTL self-heal hides stale redirect; explicit invalidation via version token is the real fix
One alert: DB pool utilization >80% sustained -- earliest direct precursor to API unavailability
Live check (progress/verify_m6.py): created link WM6y7T -> GET /r/WM6y7T 302 -> DELETE 204 -> GET /r/WM6y7T 404 immediately, no stale redirect
